newsitem.title: USA: U.S. insists NATO open to ex-Soviet states.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insists NATO open to ex-Soviet states.

text.p: The United States remains adamant that former Soviet republics will not be barred from NATO membership, a senior U.S. official said on Friday.
The official, briefing wire service reporters ahead of next week's U.S.-Russia summit, was responding to President Boris Yeltsin's stepped-up opposition to alliance membership for ex-Soviet states.
"It won't happen. It'll never happen. When Russians say you, the United States, have to agree with us that not one square inch of Soviet territory will ever be in NATO, we say no," the official said.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, also said the United States remained opposed to any specified lengthy pause in NATO taking on additional members after a first post-Cold War group of new entrants is decided in July.

Yeltsin is to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton next Wednesday and on Thursday in Helsinki. Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is due in Washington on Saturday through Monday for crucial talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and other officials that could decide if the summit is a success or failure.

Spurgeon Keeney, director of the private Arms Control Association, said on Friday the Helsinki summit was one of the most important of the post-Cold War era and would set the tone for U.S.-Russian ties during Clinton's second term of office.

He and other experts warned that if Moscow and Washington were unable to resolve their thorny differences on NATO enlargement and the START II strategic nuclear arms reduction treaty, the international arms control could start unravelling.

NATO's 16 leaders plan a July summit in Madrid to decide on new members. Poland , Hungary and the Czech republic are the top contenders but Romania and Slovenia also are under discussion. The senior official insisted Washington was still open to Romania and Slovenia.

In Moscow on Friday, Yeltsin said the Helsinki summit would be the hardest since he became Russian president in 1991 and he said the one "categoric condition" for Russia was that NATO should not try to draw in any of the 12 former Soviet republics which make up the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) or the Baltic states of Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia.
"We are not ruling out anybody," the U.S. official said.
Russia and some Europeans raised the idea of a specified pause, maybe even as long as 10 years, in NATO taking on more members after a first group was invited to join in July.
The senior U.S. official acknowledged that practically speaking it would take a couple of years before NATO was ready and able to accept another group of new members.

But as for a specified formal pause, "we hate it ... It suggests that there was something precipitous and imprudent about enlargement to begin with, which there was not. It suggests that we owe the Russians something for having done the first tranche, which we do not," he said.

In an effort to calm Moscow's fears about an expanded NATO being a threat to Russian security, the alliance is negotiating with Moscow a charter or document ensuring enhanced cooperation between NATO and Russia that could be signed at a separate NATO-Russia summit before Madrid.
Russia has been demanding a "legally binding" document to be ratified by the legislatures of all NATO member states. The senior U.S. official said on Friday: "It's not going to happen."
Instead, "we're proposing a high-level, highly public, highly significant political commitment a la the (1972) Shanghai communique" which governs U.S. relations with China to this day, he said.

The United States is willing to have a NATO-Russia charter, establish a NATO-Russia consultative council and change the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe treaty to meet Russian security concerns, the official said.

But he said Washington was "unbending" in opposing a delay in NATO enlargement, a Russian veto over NATO decision-making, second-class membership for new NATO members and NATO being subordinated to any group, such as the U.N. Security Council.
